title: Instruction Fine-Tuning with LoRA & QLoRA
summary: How LoRA's low-rank update and QLoRA's 4-bit storage change what fine-tuning costs, which choices the evidence says actually matter -- adapter placement, loss masking, dataset suitability -- and how to ship adapters merged or swappable without losing track of the base model they depend on.
objectives: Explain LoRA's reparameterization -- a frozen weight matrix plus a trainable low-rank update scaled by alpha over r -- and why a merged adapter adds no inference latency.
Explain QLoRA's split between a 4-bit storage data type and a 16-bit computation data type, and what NF4, double quantization, and paged optimizers each contribute.
Choose adapter placement, rank, and alpha from the evidence reported in the LoRA and QLoRA papers rather than from habit.
Configure instruction-tuning loss masking and chat templates so the model is trained on responses rather than prompts.
Decide whether to merge an adapter or serve it separately, given batching, task-switching, and quantization-backend constraints.

sections.title: The low-rank update: freeze W0, train BA
paragraphs: Full fine-tuning retrains every parameter, and the LoRA paper (Hu et al.) uses GPT-3 175B to show why that stops scaling: deploying an independent fine-tuned instance per task, each with 175B parameters, is prohibitively expensive. LoRA freezes the pre-trained weights and injects trainable rank-decomposition matrices into the Transformer's layers. The motivating hypothesis is that the change in weights during adaptation has a low 'intrinsic rank', so it can be represented by two small matrices instead of a full-size update.

Concretely, for a frozen weight matrix W0 the forward pass becomes h = W0x + BAx, where B and A are the only trained parameters. The paper initializes A with random Gaussian values and B with zeros, so the update BA is zero at the start and training begins exactly at the base model's behaviour. The update is scaled by alpha / r; the authors set alpha to the first r they tried and did not tune it, because the scaling reduces the need to retune hyperparameters when r changes. Hugging Face PEFT's default, which it describes as matching the reference implementation, initializes A with Kaiming-uniform values rather than the Gaussian described in the paper's text (B is still zero); a Gaussian option is available, and use_rslora=True switches the scale to alpha / sqrt(r).

The paper reports that, against GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA reduced trainable parameters by 10,000 times and GPU memory by 3 times, while performing on par with or better than full fine-tuning on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3. Those are the paper's measurements on its tasks -- a reason to try LoRA, not a guarantee for yours.
sections.callout: Because B starts at zero, a LoRA run that has not learned anything yet is the base model. Any behaviour change you see is, by construction, the adapter.

sections.title: Where adapters go matters more than how big they are
paragraphs: The LoRA paper limited its study to attention weights and froze the MLP modules for simplicity. Under a fixed parameter budget on GPT-3, adapting both the query and value projections gave the best overall performance, putting the whole budget into the query or key projection alone was significantly worse, and a rank as small as 1 was enough for query-plus-value on WikiSQL and MultiNLI while adapting the query projection alone needed a larger rank. The authors conclude that it is preferable to adapt more weight matrices than to adapt a single type of weight with a larger rank.

The QLoRA paper (Dettmers et al.) reached a compatible conclusion on instruction tuning with a different model family. For LLaMA 7B on Alpaca, it found the most critical LoRA hyperparameter was how many adapters are used in total: LoRA on all linear transformer-block layers was required to match full fine-tuning performance, while other hyperparameters such as the rank r did not affect performance. Its reported settings were r = 64, alpha = 16, with adapters on all linear layers.

The PEFT conceptual guide still describes applying LoRA to attention blocks only as the typical choice, while the QLoRA-style recipe in PEFT's quantization guide sets target_modules to 'all-linear'. The shared lesson from both papers is that spreading adapters across more of the model's matrices mattered more than raising the rank on a few of them. Treat that as the first hypothesis to test on your task, not as a setting to copy.

code.label: A LoRA configuration using the QLoRA paper's reported settings
code.code:
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

config = LoraConfig(
    r=64,                        # QLoRA paper setting
    lora_alpha=16,               # scale = lora_alpha / r = 0.25
    lora_dropout=0.1,            # paper: 0.1 up to 13B, 0.05 for 33B/65B
    target_modules="all-linear", # adapters on every linear layer
    bias="none",
)
model = get_peft_model(base_model, config)

sections.title: QLoRA: 4-bit storage, 16-bit computation
paragraphs: QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized model into LoRA adapters, and the paper reports that this cut memory enough to fine-tune a 65B-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit fine-tuning task performance. The mechanism is a split between data types: weights are stored in a low-precision storage type, usually 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), and dequantized to a computation type, usually BFloat16, whenever they are used in a matrix multiplication. Weight gradients are computed only for the LoRA parameters.

Three techniques carry the memory savings. NF4 is a 4-bit data type the paper describes as information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights; in its experiments NF4 with double quantization matched 16-bit LoRA on MMLU, while 4-bit float lagged by about one percentage point. Double quantization quantizes the quantization constants themselves: at a block size of 64, it reduces their overhead from 0.5 bits per parameter to about 0.127, a saving of roughly 0.373 bits per parameter. Paged optimizers use NVIDIA unified memory to evict optimizer state to CPU RAM when the GPU runs out of memory and page it back for the update step, so that memory spikes during gradient checkpointing do not cause out-of-memory errors.

In PEFT, the QLoRA recipe is a BitsAndBytesConfig with load_in_4bit, the nf4 quant type, double quantization, and a bfloat16 compute dtype, followed by prepare_model_for_kbit_training before the adapter is attached. PEFT also offers LoftQ initialization, which starts the LoRA weights so as to minimize quantization error; it requires loading the base model unquantized for initialization, and PEFT recommends targeting as many layers as possible when using it.

code.label: Loading a base model for QLoRA-style training with PEFT
code.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import prepare_model_for_kbit_training

bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",              # storage data type
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,         # quantize the quantization constants
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,  # computation data type
)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID, quantization_config=bnb_config)
model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)
# then attach the LoraConfig from the previous section with get_peft_model

sections.title: Instruction data: train on the response, not the prompt
paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning minimizes the negative log-likelihood of target tokens, and the practical question is which tokens count as targets. In Hugging Face TRL's SFTTrainer, a prompt-completion dataset computes loss on the completion tokens only by default (completion_only_loss); a conversational dataset can be restricted to assistant turns with assistant_only_loss=True, which needs a chat template containing generation markers -- TRL patches the template automatically for known model families. Padding tokens are always excluded through an ignore index. For conversational data the trainer applies the chat template itself; for base models that already ship a chat template, TRL notes the EOS token must be aligned with that template so responses terminate correctly.

The QLoRA paper provides evidence for masking. Across four instruction datasets with a 7B model and 52,000 examples, training only on the target response was beneficial to MMLU compared with also training on the instruction; the authors note they did not measure the effect on chatbot benchmarks. The same paper found dataset suitability mattered more than dataset size: growing a dataset or training for more epochs moved MMLU only marginally, while the differences between datasets were far larger. It also observed that benchmark results likely depend on how similar the fine-tuning data is to the benchmark -- FLAN v2 did well on MMLU and worst on the Vicuna chatbot benchmark.

TRL logs loss, mean_token_accuracy, entropy, and grad_norm during training, and notes that adapter training typically uses a higher learning rate (around 1e-4) because only the new parameters are being learned. A falling training loss tells you the model is fitting your targets. Whether that is the behaviour you wanted is a question only a held-out evaluation from your target task can answer.
sections.callout: Your dataset chooses what the model learns; the loss mask chooses which of its tokens are allowed to teach. Get both wrong and a clean loss curve still describes the wrong model.

sections.title: Shipping: merge, swap, or keep separate
paragraphs: LoRA's linear form allows the update to be folded into the base weights for deployment -- W = W0 + BA -- so a merged model runs with no additional inference latency, which the paper contrasts with adapter layers. Switching tasks means subtracting BA and adding a different B'A', a quick operation with little memory overhead. The paper's storage example is stark: with r = 4 on only the query and value projections, the GPT-3 checkpoint shrank from about 350 GB to 35 MB, which is what makes keeping many task adapters around a single base model practical.

Merging has a cost the paper names directly: once A and B are absorbed into W, it is no longer straightforward to batch inputs for different tasks, each needing different A and B, in one forward pass. Leaving adapters unmerged and choosing them per sample remains possible where latency is not critical. PEFT exposes both paths: merge_and_unload() produces a standalone merged model, merge_adapter() and unmerge_adapter() toggle merging while keeping the PeftModel, unload() recovers the base model, and add_weighted_adapter() combines several LoRAs into a new one.

The quantization backend can decide for you. PEFT documents that adapters trained on AQLM-quantized models must be saved separately because merging with AQLM weights is not possible, and that merge() and unmerge() are not supported for INC-quantized models. Before promising a merged artifact, confirm the backend supports it -- and in every case record the exact base model and quantization configuration alongside the adapter, because an adapter is an update to one specific set of frozen weights.

activity.title: Run a QLoRA experiment you can defend
instructions: Choose a small open base model and an instruction dataset of a few thousand examples in prompt-completion or conversational format. Record the base model identifier and its exact revision.
Configure 4-bit NF4 storage with double quantization and a bfloat16 compute dtype, and a LoRA adapter on all linear layers. Record r, alpha, and the resulting scale.
Train two variants that differ in exactly one factor: either loss masking on (completion-only or assistant-only) versus off, or adapters on attention projections only versus all linear layers.
Evaluate both variants on a held-out set drawn from your target task, plus a small general-capability check, and keep the training-loss, mean-token-accuracy, and grad-norm curves for both runs.

Decide whether to deploy each adapter merged or separately, based on how you expect to serve it: one task per endpoint, many tasks sharing one base model, or a quantization backend that constrains merging.
evidence: A configuration record: base model and revision, quantization settings, LoRA r, alpha, and target modules, loss-masking setting, and learning rate.
Training curves for both variants with a note on where, if anywhere, they diverge.
A held-out comparison table and a one-paragraph merge-or-separate decision naming the serving constraint that drove it.
activity.reflectionPrompt: One of your two variants probably reached a lower training loss. What evidence convinced you whether it is actually the better model, and what about your held-out data could have reversed that answer?

questions.prompt: Why does a freshly initialized LoRA adapter leave the model's behaviour exactly equal to the base model's?
choices: Because A is initialized to the identity matrix
Because B is initialized to zero, so the update BA is zero at the start of training
Because the base weights are copied into A and B
Because alpha is set to zero until training starts
questions.explanation: The LoRA paper initializes A randomly and B to zero, so the update BA starts at zero; PEFT's default also initializes B to zero, producing an identity transform.

questions.prompt: In QLoRA, which statement correctly describes the data types used?
choices: All weights and gradients are kept in 4-bit precision throughout training
Weights are stored in 4-bit NF4 and dequantized to BFloat16 for computation; weight gradients are computed only for the LoRA parameters
Weights are stored in BFloat16 and computed in 4-bit
Only the LoRA adapters are quantized to 4-bit
questions.explanation: QLoRA uses one storage data type (usually 4-bit NormalFloat) and one computation data type (usually BFloat16), dequantizing for each forward and backward pass while computing weight gradients only for the adapters.

questions.prompt: According to the QLoRA paper's LLaMA 7B experiments, which LoRA choice was most critical to matching full fine-tuning performance?
choices: Using the largest possible rank r
Applying LoRA to all linear transformer-block layers, which sets how many adapters are used in total
Tuning alpha independently for every layer
Adapting only the query projection
questions.explanation: The paper reports that the total number of adapters was the most critical hyperparameter and that LoRA on all linear layers was required to match full fine-tuning, while r did not affect performance in that setting.

questions.prompt: You train TRL's SFTTrainer on a prompt-completion dataset without changing any loss settings. Which tokens contribute to the loss?
choices: Every token, prompt and completion alike
Only the completion tokens, because completion_only_loss is the default for prompt-completion data
Only the prompt tokens
Only the final token of each example
questions.explanation: For prompt-completion datasets TRL computes the loss on completion tokens by default; set completion_only_loss=False to train on the full sequence. Padding is always excluded.

questions.prompt: You serve twenty task-specific adapters from one base model, and a single batch mixes requests for different tasks. Why is merging each adapter into the base weights a poor fit?
choices: Merged adapters add inference latency
Once A and B are absorbed into W, batching inputs that need different adapters in one forward pass is no longer straightforward
Merging is impossible for LoRA
Merged models cannot be saved to disk
questions.explanation: The LoRA paper names this limitation: merging removes latency but makes mixed-task batching difficult; keeping adapters unmerged and selecting them per sample remains possible where latency is not critical.

questions.prompt: What does QLoRA's double quantization quantize, and roughly what does it save?
choices: The activations; about 4 bits per parameter
The quantization constants; about 0.373 bits per parameter at a block size of 64
The LoRA adapters; about half their size
The optimizer states; all of their memory
questions.explanation: Double quantization quantizes the constants used by the first quantization, cutting their overhead from 0.5 to about 0.127 bits per parameter at block size 64 -- a saving of about 0.373 bits per parameter.

Reduced-motion mode shows the diagram without animation.
